tion, and in view of the wide discussion in Manitoba and Saskatchewan as to the statement made by me in this house on July 16, regarding shipments of grain from Churchill, I desire to make absolutely clear the position of the government, which has been subjected to unfair and unjust attacks.
In the first place, the fact that we have continued to push forward the work at Churchill at great expense, so that it is ahead of schedule while other important works in Canada have not been proceeded with, proves our good faith. Secondly, being assured of the port being ready for test shipment by September 15, as arranged for in the contract by the previous government, we then endeavoured to induce grain shippers to supply cargoes on the basis that ships would be available to carry such cargoes at rates not greater-including insurance and all charges -than via present through routes. But as pointed out in my statement of July 16, we did not succeed in this effort, and the government has no machinery with which to buy grain in Canada and dispose of it in Europe.
Since making the statement, certain newspapers and organizations in western Canada have criticized us severely for alleged inaction. I have requested western grain dealers to submit any reasonable proposition they thought desirable for providing cargoes of grain for the test shipments on the basis of a freight rate not higher than the present through rates, the natural and intended inference being that we would absorb any difference in rates due to increased insurance or other charges. The only proposal I have yet received in reply has been one wire stating that 150,000 bushels of grain can be assured. This is only about half a cargo.
In view of the above let me again state our position. If a proposition is made to the government to supply from one to three cargoes of grain for shipment via Churchill, the shipper to pay rates on the basis of present through rates from the prairies to Europe via Montreal, the government will see that ships are available and absorb any difference due to insurance or other transportation charges. That surely is a fair proposal on the part of the government. Now instead of criticism or abuse let the grain trade or some responsible organization come forward with cargo proposals.
Let me add that the statement that Mr. Dunning intended sending out five million bushels as a test movement cannot be verified or substantiated either by departmental records or officials, the same officials as obtained under the late government, and furthermore such a quantity could not be shipped out via Churchill this season, as it
could not be handled between September 15 and the close of navigation.
If any action is to be taken it should be taken quickly as I am advised that vessel arrangements must be made not later than August 10.
May I just add, in regard to the statement of my hon. friend concerning Hon. Mr. Merkley, that so far we have had no proposition of any kind from this gentleman. Some days ago Mr. Merkley telegraphed me asking some questions, and I wired back telling him to put forward any proposition he might have and the government would give it fair consideration. As yet I have received no proposition from him, but if he brings forward any suggestion certainly it will be given fair and reasonable consideration in every possible way.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Minister of Justice) moved that the house go into committee on Bill No. 35, to remove the necessity of the reelection of members of the House of Commons of Canada on acceptance of office.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILL TO REMOVE NECESSITY OF BEELECTION UPON ACCEPTANCE OF OFFICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
the bill which is at present before the house as a government measure is one which the house will recognize as a bill previously introduced during this session, by an hon. member, as a private measure. As such it was considered by the house, disposed of in the course of debate and dropped from the order paper. It has made its reappearance as a government measure, and the question which naturally suggests itself to the minds of hon. members is just what circumstance has developed which has occasioned the government to take this particular measure as a means of assisting itself along its own path as the years go by. Not only was the measure disposed of at this session some weeks ago as I have indicated, but it made its appearance in parliament several times in previous years only on each occasion to disappear. When the former Liberal administration was in office the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) brought in a similar measure and the government, though it had been in office for almost eight or nine years, intimated, when last the bill was introduced, that it saw no necessity for the enactment of any such legislation. We preferred to uphold the principle that we should keep the government and the people in as close contact as possible on all matters of concern to the nation as a whole.	,
Now the present administration proposes in this measure that a member of parliament, if appointed to office as a minister of the crown, may assume office without in the first place going back to the people for reelection. The bill is entitled:
An act to remove the necessity of the reelection of members of the House of Commons of Canada on acceptance of office.
I think it should read:	"An act to remove
the necessity of the present administration having by-elections when the same at any cost can be avoided". So regarded, the measure is in keeping with what up to the present time has been the practice of the administration. We have a statute which provides that by-elections shall take place

Ministers of the Crown
within six months after the chief electoral officer has been advised that a vacancy exists in any constituency. The intention of that statute was that all constituencies should be represented in the House of Commons, and that at least within six months from the time a vacancy occurred it should be filled by election. Two elections are being held next month, one to fill a vacancy which occurred in October last, and the other to fill a vacancy which occurred early in the month of January. But throughout this entire session the two constituencies in question, one in Ontario and One in Quebec, Hamilton East and Three Rivers-St. Maurice have not been represented at all in this House of Commons. The government of the day is responsible for that fact, and there must be a good and sufficient reason in the mind of the administration for its having hesitated to bring on by-elections in time to permit of the representation of these constituencies.
No doubt the Prime Minister is anxious to make certain Changes in the administration. He has intimated to parliament that he does not intend to continue in the office of Minister of Finance. I presume that one of the objects of the bill is to enable him to bring into the ministry as Minister of Finance some hon. member he has in mind, to have him assume the office without the necessity of going back to the people for reelection. I imagine that what he will do will be to make one of his present colleagues Minister of Finance and then bring in some hon. member to fill the portfolio thus left vacant. At any rate, it is quite clear that the administration has to a very considerable extent lost confidence in itself, or it would not hesitate to appoint a new minister and let him go before his constituents for reelection in the usual way, it would seek the approbation of the electorate, as has been customary in this country from the days of confederation to the present time.
There are, I think, the strongest reasons why under representative institutions the government should seek an expression of the people's views as intimately and as frequently as the customary procedure of the constitution provides. The hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) will probably tell us, if he speaks on the measure, that Great Britain has adopted a course similar to that proposed in this measure. There, since 1926, a newly elected minister is not obliged, if he holds a seat in the House of Commons, to go back for re-election. But there were two stages in effecting that change in the British system. The first change was to limit the time within
which a minister who was a member might assume office without vacating his seat to the period of nine months after a general election. It was in 1919 that the British Act was first amended and amended in this way. It was felt that where immediately after a general election a government had been formed there was not the same necessity for' a minister of the crown to go back for reelection; and the act as it then stood was amended to provide that if a new minister took office within nine months after a general election he should not be obliged to go back for reelection. But it was not until seven years after that, in 1926, that the nine month limitation was removed. I suggest that if this measure is to carry at all it should provide the same limitation that was enacted in Great Britain when the British act was first amended.
I was interested in some of the reasons given at the time the act was amended against the change, and one paragraph in the speech of Sir John Marriott delivered in the British House of Commons on February 12, 1926, is so much to the point that I shall read it. It contains, in a word, all that I would say at this moment on the measure. Sir John Marriott said ;
I want to suggest whether at this particular moment in the evolution of our constitution- and now, as always, our constitution is changing udth very great rapidity-it is really wise to do anything that will further disturb the equilibrium of the constitution in favour of the executive and against the legislature on the one side and the electorate on the other.
That question, I think, may be asked with great pertinency with reference to constitutional development in' this country to-day. Great Britain, as we all know, is a very compact country; the number of constituencies is large but they are all comprised within a very small area. Moreover, under the British system by-elections are brought on within a very few days and at most weeks after vacancies occur. So that in Britain there is constant opportunity for the electorate to express its views on the government's policies and the administration of the nation's affairs. With such a large number of member's of parliament, the vacancies that inevitably occur are considerably more than those in a smaller body; and there the expedition with which by-elections are brought on affords a constant expression of the nation's view as to the way in which its affairs are being administered. In Canada, and particularly since the present administration has been in office, the tendency has been more and more to increase the powers of the governor in council, to with-
Ministers of the Crown

draw from parliament those opportunities for discussion of public questions which would be available if the governor in council was not being given such excessive powers. There has been the further tendency already referred to of protracting and delaying the filling of vacancies by by-election. In these and other ways the ministry is getting further and further away from the electorate; it cannot so readily ascertain the views of the people.
But there is this further fact which I submit is of great significance in a country like Canada. We have vast stretches of territory, there are racial, religious and economic considerations of which account must be taken in so many particulars that there is an ever present necessity for a ministry to be reconciling differences which in the nature of things are inherent by seeking to get the approval of the people in as many ways as possible. One would be any important changes made in the personnel of the ministry.
If this present measure goes through it will be possible for my right hon. friend in making future appointments to the ministry if he so desires to ignore altogether considerations of geography which are very important in the formation of a ministry. It would be possible also for him to ignore altogether considerations of a religious character which are important in the formation of a ministry, having regard to the diversity of religious beliefs of the people in our country. There would be also the possibility of ignoring altogether important economic considerations. I know my right hon. friend will say that when it comes to a general election the day of reckoning will have arrived and he will then have to take responsibility for all changes made. But much of mischief may' have been wrought as a consequence in the interval. I submit that what is needed in Canada is that every important act of the ministry should inasmuch as may be possible be of a character which will not tend to emphasize differences, but which will tend to lessen them. The fact that a newly elected minister is obliged to go before the people for their approval before being permitted to continue as a member of the administration is a great safeguard in more ways than one.
It is not for me to advise the Prime Minister as to what may be in his own interest, but if he will allow me to say one word in all kindliness, it would be that I think he will find when this measure has passed that instead of his troubles being lessened they will be very greatly increased.

A moment ago I was interrupted by the hon. member lor York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson). If my right hon. friend were changing his ministry to-morrow and the hon. member for York-Sunbury wished to be taken into the ministry, in giving as a reason why this might not be possible the argument would no longer be possible on the part of the Prime Minister that account must be taken of the particular part of the country from which he comes, of the particular profession which he follows, or of the particular religious belief which he holds. The Prime Minister will find that what is true with respect to one hon. member will [DOT] be equally true with respect to all hon. members on his side of the chamber. Every hon. gentleman opposite should realize that once this measure passes whatever there formerly was in the way of necessary consideration on the part of the Prime Minister as to how the country is likely to view his appointment, will have largely disappeared. The Prime Minister will find increasingly that this is so in the minds of his followers. I am inclined to believe that that is something which my right hon. friend will discover to be even truer than at the moment he may believe to be the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BILL TO REMOVE NECESSITY OF BEELECTION UPON ACCEPTANCE OF OFFICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not desire to delay
the house during the preliminary stages of this bill, except to say that the reason why this bill has been taken over is that it is sound in principle and its application will be found to be beneficial in this country just as it has been in every other British dominion as well as in the motherland. The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) who, in the absence of the original sponsor, moved the second reading of this bill, gave a very careful and full statement of the reasons why such legislation should be placed upon the statute books. Those who heard him speak were convinced of the soundness of his argument; those who did not hear him speak should read his remarks in Hansard.
The law now upon the statute book of Canada had its origin in the seventeenth century when there was probably a sound reason for the maintenance of such a rule. In those days the influence of the sovereign was very powerful and the subjects were very jealous of their rights. They demanded that no favourite of the king should be appointed to office without first giving them an opportunity of pronouncing upon the individual. This law arose from an effort of the people to maintain their rights against royal encroachment.

Ministers oj the Crown

subtopic: BILL TO REMOVE NECESSITY OF BEELECTION UPON ACCEPTANCE OF OFFICE
speechtext:
If my
speech was so immensely convincing, as the minister so flatteringly says it was, why was it that on that occasion I could not get any support from my hon. friend or those around him?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BILL TO REMOVE NECESSITY OF BEELECTION UPON ACCEPTANCE OF OFFICE
speechtext:
We on this side of the
house thought that the bill was moving so smoothly and in the proper direction that we should not interfere with its passage, and we hope that it may move just as smoothly on the present occasion.
In those early days when this law was first introduced into the British parliament, members of parliament were not paid any salary or remuneration. They served freely in the parliament of Great Britain and it was thought that, having been elected under conditions which prevented their accepting salaries, when they obtained positions of emolument under the crown they should go back to the people in order that the people might ratify the appointments and agree to the emolument. Members of this parliament have at all times been in receipt of emolument so there was no reason for the adoption of this law in Canada. My right hon. friend stated that I probably would refer to the fact that in Great Britain and the other dominions this ancient law had been abrogated some time ago. Any hon. member who reads the bill will see these facts all set out in the explanatory note.
In 1919, Great Britain practically abrogated the law, but included a nine months limitation which provided that for nine months after a general election members of parliament upon, being called to the cabinet should not be required to go back for reelection. That law worked for the succeeding seven years but it was then found that there was no necessity for the nine months limitation, and the parliament of Great Britain, in 1926, deliberately repealed that limitation. Now the law in England does not require that a member who has been called to the government go back for reelection, neither is this required in South Africa, Australia, New Zealand, the Irish Free State or in any other British dominion so far as I am aware. Why then in this parliament should we hold on to this antiquated statute? The hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) introduced this bill once or twice in previous sessions, but for some reason or another the bill was never pushed to a conclusion. The hon. member for Cartier seemed to have rested on his oars for some reason best known to himself, and the bill never advanced to its second reading.
But the time has come when we believe we should put ourselves in line with the legislation of the rest of the British Empire in this respect. My right hon. friend's chief objection to this bill seems to be to its title. He imagines that it might more properly be called a measure to relieve the present government of the embarrassment of by-elections. I do not think this government fears anything or has anything to fear at this particular time in regard to by-elections. Let me tell my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition that a by-election is pending in East Hamilton and the Liberal party is not even represented in that constituency. I am inclined to think it may be some little time hence before the Liberal party is seriously represented in electoral constituencies in the Dominion of Canada.
There are, however, some very sound reasons for the adoption of a measure such as this. We urge it, first, on the ground of convenience ; second, on the ground of expediency, and third on the ground of saving of expense. Those are three strong reasons for supporting this proposal. We know the delay in bringing on elections in this country is very great. I am told that in Great Britain a writ can be issued and a man be returned and take his seat in parliament in twenty-one days. In Canada this takes two months. This delay is very inconvenient. The expense of elections is very heavy.

The country did lose his services for the time being; and" what happened in the case of so illustrious a statesman as Sir Wilfrid Laurier might happen again in connection with his successors. I am pointing out that it is a matter of inconvenience to a government, to parliament; it is a loss to the country to be deprived of the services of a man under such conditions. It may not and did not in that case affect a majority in the house, but it does affect the conduct of affairs in the Dominion of Canada. There is no sound reason for retaining the rule and there are very sound reasons for doing away with it. For those reasons we ask that the bill be now passed.
Mr. ARMAND LaVERGNE:	(Montmagny): I listened to the address of the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) when he introduced this bill, and when the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) was speaking I was wondering whether he would say if he were in favour of the measure or not. Perhaps it was due to lack of understanding or poor hearing on my part, but I am not quite sure whether the leader of the opposition is in favour of this legislation or not. Probably, before asking this side of the house the reasons for such a bill, he might put his question to the hon. member for Cartier.
I have listened to the Minister of. Justice (Mr. Guthrie) ' and I have heard his three reasons and the example cited. I am not supposed to be a democrat; on the contrary I am supposed to be a very strong Conservative ; but being a Conservative I am in favour of the rights of the people being maintained, and I cannot see why a man who has been given a portfolio should not have to go back to the people to have his appointment confirmed. The fact that this rule has been abolished in Great Britain, the Irish Free State or South Africa is no reason to me. The important point of this bill is what

is good for Canada. I believe, representing what I think are the rights of the people to approve the choice of a minister, they are the masters of the administration and no government should give a portfolio carrying a salary and the confidence of the government to anyone without its action being approved by the people. I think the measure brought forward by the hon. member for Cartier, this foundling left on the steps of the government, should not be adopted by the government. We are going against the rights of the people, against the constitution, against our institutions bj' adopting such a bill. I am only a very ordinary, humble member; I do not expect ever to be a minister of the crown, but I think any man who is chosen as a minister should not be chosen without having the approbation of the people, and he should resign his seat in order to stand for reelection. If the people reject him, they are the master and he should not be a minister. Therefore I am going to vote against the bill.

subtopic: BILL TO REMOVE NECESSITY OF BEELECTION UPON ACCEPTANCE OF OFFICE
speechtext:
It is very interesting to follow debates on matters of this kind which have reference to historical developments. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) has been interesting on this point, but I think he missed one historical connecting link. The measure as adopted in England was not based on the old claims of the people to control nominations. On the contrary, it was based on what happened after the revolution of 1688. As everyone knows or ought to know who intends to be faithful to British precedents and history, after the revolution there was an assertion on the part of the House of Commons as against both the claims of the crown and the claims of the House of Lords. Eventually the House of Commons came to be dominated largely by the nominees of the great Whig families who controlled most of the rotten boroughs, and, under the reign of George III, by the favourites of the crown. This measure in England, if I remember right -I am speaking from memory, and old memory-was enacted at the time of the reaction against the old Whig rule. The Reform movement was largely supported by Edmund Burke, and later on by Charles James Fox, and there came a time when the House of Commons was largely composed of the nominees either of the great aristocratic families or of the crown . It was not a question of official emolument, nor was it a question of official position under the crown. It was a question of influence.

The reaction showed that the enactment of a *statute is not sufficient to protect the liberties of the people or the independence of members of the House of Commons. Eventually when the reaction came on, curiously enough it was supported by such statesmen as Chatham and later by Edmund Burke, more or less connected with the old Tory tradition. They reacted against the Whig influence.
But to go into that would carry us too far. I think it is better to take the conditions as they are in Canada at the present time. For my part I have supported the principle of this measure ever since it was first introduced into this house by the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) in 1926, and I have seen no reason to change my views because the parties have changed sides. I was in favour of this measure when the Liberals were in power, and I am still in favour of it now that the Tories are in power, whether it favours one government or the other.
As far as the rights of the people are concerned. they are exercised in a general election. Then the people have an opportunity to show their mind when they vote for one party or the other, rightly or wrongly. Once a party is in power I do not see why choosing one member of the House of Commons or one member of the Senate to become a member of the administration should necessitate reelection for his maintenance in office. If the Prime Minister chooses one member of the House of Commons to fill a vacant office in his cabinet, I do not see how the people at large in the country have a chance of expressing their views for or against the policies of the government in a bye-election, which will be held in one single constituency, for the election of that particular member. In that regard I think the argument made by the right hon. leader of the opposition falls entirely short of the question. He says that there are considerations of geography and considerations of religion. I do not see what
religion has to do with it, but I suppose he meant that the Prime Minister could choose a member of the house from one province or another to fill a vacancy. Well, after he has been chosen, I do not see what difference it makes to have to submit to reelection. If, for example, he has been chosen from Ontario to fill an office that has been vacated by a member from Quebec, it is not likely that he will offer himself for reelection in the province of Quebec, and so I do not see what chance the people of Quebec would have to vote against the choice of the Prime Minister from amongst his Ontario membership. If the new minister had to be reelected at large, there would be a kind of plebiscite which might allow an expression of opinion to the people at large; but since he has to be reelected in his own constituency, it is a hundred to one that he will stand a much better chance of being reelected as minister than as a private member of parliament.

speechtext: My hon. friend has not caught the point I had in mind. He speaks of religion. In the same way a ministry might become an entirely western or an entirely eastern ministry, or a ministry composed entirely of lawyers, or agriculturists or manufacturers or some other class, without any opportunity of being given to the people to pass upon it so long as a parliament lasts.

I do not suppose any Prime Minister, either our present Mussolini, or the right hon. leader of the opposition, if he has a chance of coming back to power, or any other Prime Minister, would be foolish enough to resort to such a practice as the right hon. gentleman has suggested. But if he did, what chance would all the Ro-man Catholics of Canada, for example, have to express their disapproval of one Protestant minister taking the place of a Roman Catholic when that minister was being reelected in a Protestant constituency? They

would have no chance at all; their chance would be in a general election.
On various occasions I have endeavoured to bring back the minds of the house to this fact, that after all the only safeguard which the people at large have is at a general election. A by-e'lection where a member of the government who is already a member of the House of Commons goes back to his own constituency for reelection affords very little relief to the people at large, in the nine provinces of Canada, belonging to this creed or that creed, this race or that race, this class or that class, or very little opportunity to express their opinion. On the other hand, I can see the practical results of this measure, the effect of which will be to avoid at least one by-election. I believe one of the curses under which this country of ours, as well as the neighbouring republic, is suffering, is in having too many elections, general elections and by-elections. We have municipal elections, provincial elections, and federal elections. There is almost no year in the life of a parliament, and hardly any month in any year in which some part of our country is not disturbed with political and electoral agitation. Of course, we are bound to have it, but once we have had a consultation of the people at large at the proper time and they have made their choice as to the party that should rule and the government that should be formed, I think the less we have of electoral agitation and the less going back to this or that particular constituency the better. I cannot see that the reelection of one or two members of a government for this or that constituency gives any indication of the attitude of mind of the millions of electors in the Dominion of Canada from one ocean to the other. I cannot see the significance of a by-election as far as the general policies of the government are concerned. I repeat, when the hon. member for Cartier introduced a similar bill on a former occasion I supported it, and nothing has developed in the meantime to prevent me from supporting the measure once more.

member or as a Progressive and he joined the Conservative government, surely his electors would have a right to say whether or not they would support him in his new political attitude.

I think in that regard this measure would be very satisfactory, but if a government has been in power a couple of years and fails to redeem a great part of its promises and brings down legislation which was not contemplated, before an hon. member becomes a member of the cabinet he should be forced to go back to his electors for their approval.

speechtext:
When the fathers of confederation framed the constitution of this country they had in mind government by the people for the people, and they took every means in their power to see that the people would have absolute control of this parliament. I would say, Mr. Speaker, that immediately following a general election it should not be necessary for an hon. member to go back to his constituency for reelection if he accepts office in a cabinet formed by his own party; I would have no objection to the removal of the necessity for reelection in a case of that kind.
There comes to my mind the occasion in 1877 when Sir Wilfrid Laurier went back to his constituents for reelection. The country was passing through an economic crisis at that time, and when the by-election took place the Conservative party, led by the late Hon. Mr. Tarte, who subsequently became Minister of Public Works, fought Sir Wilfrid day and night, to the great surprise of the [DOT]country and to the dismay of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. That was one instance when the people were given an opportunity to pronounce a verdict. Another instance which comes to my mind is that of the resignation of a minister from the northwest in 1905, when the western provinces were incorporated. At that time I had the honour to be deputy speaker of this house, and a new minister had to be elected from the west. The minister elected was Hon. Mr. Oliver, who had to go back to the electors following his appointment to the cabinet.
We have made exceptions to this rule of requiring the reelection of ministers; the [DOT]deputy speaker, and the leader of the opposition, are not required to follow this procedure. Those exceptions have been made by
fMr. Rinfret.]
the internal management of this house, for reasons which are obvious. In the explanation given with regard to this bill it was stated that in the British parliament and in several of the dominions reelection is not required and I may say that the same thing applies in France also. In that country the government changes every ninety days, on an average, but the ministers are not required to go to the people; parliament is elected for a stated period, and the members remain in office even after their appointment to the cabinet.
I believe that if a member who was elected on July 28 last to support a particular policy and a particular party, to-morrow or six months or a year from now walks over to the other side of the house and accepts a portfolio with a different party, it is only fair that his constituents, whose representative he is, should be consulted on the new stand he takes. The downfall of governments has been brought about by such things; in 1879 the government of Quebec was defeated because three or four members who had been elected as Liberals walked across to the other side of the house.
I would be prepared to do away with the necessity for the reelection of ministers within say three or four months after a general election, but beyond that I think we should stand by the old principle and not abrogate in these democratic days the control of the people over this parliament. It is imperative that this control should be maintained. The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) seems to be maturing with age; I remember that in 1899 he resigned from this house in protest against the sending of a contingent to South Africa. He appealed to the electors of Labelle, and in the by-election which took place he was reelected. He took the stand that the people had not been consulted and that this should have been done before such a step was taken. That is another instance of the usefulness of these by-elections, and I think in the interests of the administration itself it should be able at times to feel the pulse of the electors in any part of the country. For these reasons, if the bill is not modified I shall have to vote against it, but if it is amended to cover only a short period after a general election I am prepared to support it.

the days before responsible government. If I understand constitutional history aright it seems to me that Lord Dufferin first laid down the principle that a cabinet minister must be elected by and be responsible to the people. At that time cabinet ministers were not necessarily chosen from a legislative body, and it seems to me that safeguard was required at that time. But that time has gone by; after a member is elected to this house surely it should not be necessary for him to go back to the people for reelection.
Let us suppose, for instance, that the present government lost the confidence of this house and were defeated by an adverse vote. That should not necessarily mean a general election. If the right hon. leader of the opposition were voted into office I contend that he should be able to carry on the government of the country as long as he enjoyed the confidence of parliament. But in the present situation that would not be possible, and it seems to me that this condition of affairs should be removed. When a government is voted into office the Prime Minister almost invariably finds it necessary to reconstruct his cabinet to some extent. He wishes to bring in men who have not appeared before the people in the election as cabine t ministers. Although elected, the moment they are called upon to assume office, they must go back to the people for reelection. It may be necessary to call parliament at the earliest possible date, but delay is inevitable because of by-elections. I regard this as a reform long overdue.

The leader of the party having a majority occupies no constitutional position -it is purely a matter of tradition and habit -but he chooses his colleagues and they go back to the people to be reelected as members of the cabinet. The amendment suggested by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) would be clearer than that proposed by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe). The theory of the former is that once elected, for five years a party will d)o whatever it pleases and if the people are not satisfied they can turn it out of office. I am surprised, not to say astonished at the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa). I remember his having stated some time ago that he believed in the importance of by-elections as a means of teaching the government a lesson at certain times and giving to the people an opportunity of pronouncing on the actions of the government during a term of parliament. I must admit that I was convinced then by the hon. member for Labelle, but now it seems that everything is changed. I am probably one of the last monarchists left, I will not say in the house, but perhaps in the country at large. The hon. member for Labelle seems to have changed his viewpoint because in 1926, if my memory serves me aright, he denounced the use of the prerogative of the sovereign to turn out a government and call upon somebody else to form one. According to him the sovereign was only what we call in French "un roi-soliveau," that is, a king who had 22110-2004
no rights and no powers of intervention, or of interference with the affairs of the nation. But to-day it seems that the rights of the people are not recognized any more. I am prepared to support the amendment of the hon. member for Quebec East as a "pis aller."
I speak as a man who 'believes in the prerogatives of the sovereign on the one side and the prerogatives of the people on the other. That is the beauty of British institutions. I do not see why in our country of liberty and freedom we should pass a measure which would entitle the sovereign to call a minister who would not be subject to the approval of the people. We are told that after a general election this approval is not necessary. That may or may not be true, still I believe the people should be consulted and should have an opportunity to express their opinion in regard to the formation of a cabinet; but if we cannot have that, I shall accept the amendment of the hon. member for Quebec East.
A moment ago I quoted the instance of the' late Mr. Dobell. He was a Conservative,-elected as a Conservative in the constituency' of Quebec West, who joined the Laurier" cabinet. If he accepted a portfolio, I am inclined to think the people of Quebec West who had elected him as a Conservative were entitled to pronounce upon his change of allegiance and upon his acceptance of the Liberal doctrines of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Being a Conservative in doctrine and a monarchist in sentiment, I maintain that the best guarantees of our freedom are to uphold the age-old and age-tested principles of the British constitution involving at- the same time the rights of the sovereign and the rights of the people. To-day. when we see thrones tottering, when we see in different countries the great institution of monarchy declining we can say as British subjects that what has made the greatness of England and of the British Empire is the maintenance of age-old and age-tested institutions, on the one side the rights of the sovereign and on the other the sovereign rights of the people. They make for the liberty of the nation; they are the guarantees of the freedom of the people and we should adhere to those principles which underlie the British constitution

principles which have given freedom to the world.

subtopic: PROPOSED ANNUAL EXPENDITURE OF $750,000 CONDITIONAL UPON AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
Let me quote from the debate. As reported in Hansard of December 6, 1909, at page 10612, I spoke, as follows. This was not a year or so after but at the very time the motion was introduced:
Mr. Mackenzie King (Minister of Labour): Mr. Speaker, I feel that I am only voicing the opinion of every member of this house when I say that our thanks are due to the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) for having brought this important subject to the attention of parliament and for the exceptionally able, forceful and comprehensive manner in which he introduced his resolution. I think, too, sir, the house is to be congratulated on the very full discussion which has taken place on this resolution, to be congratulated because the subject is one which, no matter what view we may take as to the jurisdiction of this government or a provincial government to deal with it, cannot be viewed other than as one of great national concern.
Then a little further on, having pointed out the importance of the subject as one of national concern, I continued as follows as reported at page 1076:
I think, the risk should not be run of raising a great constitutional question in a matter of such great national importance until at least the exact position of this government with regard to this question is fully and rightly understood by the different provinces and by the people in the country.
Then a little further on I said:
But I am not so sure that the exclusive right to make laws with regard to education means the right to exclude the Dominion from gathering information on any subject which may be deemed a subject of national importance. However, that may be a debatable constitutional question, and in view of the importance of the subject of this discussion, I think it would be well if the mover of this resolution would allow the government a further opportunity to consider the question from this point of view, and not press it to a division to-night.
Then a little later:
I hope that one of the results of this debate will be that the true relationship of the provinces to the Dominion on this question of great national concern will be brought out in bolder and clearer relief than ever before, and if the subject be brought up again, as I hope it will be, there will be no doubt in the mind of any member of this house, or in any group of responsible persons outside, as to whether or not the Dominion would be trespassing in endeavouring to cooperate with the provinces 

for it is cooperation alone that would be expected-to the extent the mover of this resolution would desire. I would beg to move therefore the adjournment of the debate.
The purpose of the adjournment of the debate, as is shown clearly there, was to get over any constitutional difficulty and to enable the government of the day to communicate rvith the governments of the several provinces with respect to the commission that was to be appointed.
Now, what did my hon. friend himself say in regard to my attitude? Before I quote his words I might quote those of the late Right Hon. Mr. Fielding, who also stated the government's purpose in asking for the adjournment of the debate. On December 6, 1909, at page 1089 of Hansard, Mr. Fielding is reported as having said:
I must take exception entirely to the observation of an hon. gentleman opposite that the motion to adjourn is a motion to side-track this resolution. . . .
Speaking on the resolution the other day, the present Minister of Justice spoke of Mr. Fielding as one: who understood what the position of the Liberal government was and what its intention was with respect to this question of technical education. I am now giving him the words which he himself heard and accepted in the House of Commons at the time:
.... and while I propose to vote for the motion to adjourn, I do so on altogether a different ground. After the discussion we have had, after the abundance of information brought before the house, showing the great need of this movement in Canada, it would indeed be strange if nothing further should be done. We are all of the opinion that something should be done, and the only question is what is the better way of doing it.
Then a little further on he said:
I do not say that the Dominion parliament should not step in and assist them. 1 am going to vote for the adjournment of the debate, not for the purpose of side-tracking the matter, but that we may have further opportunity of considering. not the wdsdom of doing something, but the best way in which to do it.	*
Mr. Fielding concluded:
.... and in voting for the motion to adjourn I do so in order that we may have the oppor-
Vocational Education

government that is responsible for the services and for the raising of the money.
We have progressed very far in Canada in some fields of our industrial development and the time has now come to consider carefully, if we are going to continue, as I hope we are, the expenditure on technical education and industrial research, just how far the provincial and Dominion governments respectively should go. When some years ago the government of the day introduced an act making a contribution in the form of grants to the provinces, they fixed upon a period of ten years. At that time the industrial research work that was being carried on at Ottawa was comparatively limited. No provision was made for it by any special act of parliament, but in the course of years there were persistent representations from industrial and labour organizations in Canada, from manufacturers' associations and from departments of government, regarding the need of more highly developed research work on the part of the Dominion government. When the Liberal government was in office we were faced with the question how best that additional demand could be met. We considered that the act fixing the period of ten years had been framed expressly to enable the provinces to get on their feet. Very little had been done up to the time the act was passed and the purpose of the act was to give, the provinces a real start in technical education. We understood and the report of the commission and of the debate will show that the intention was to allow for a period during which buildings might be erected and equipped, teachers trained, staffs organized, and the work advanced to some extent. We did not believe it was intended by the parliament that enacted the measure that the grant for a period of ten years, made in that way, should be permitted to become a perpetual thing. We did feel, on the other hand, that the necessity for doing more at Ottawa in the way of providing facilities for technical and scientific research was becoming more and more apparent every day. Therefore, some years before the act expired, we notified the provinces that at the end of the ten years they must not expect the grant to be continued but must make provision for providing in their entirety the services which they had themselves started. We required additional money for federal purposes. It was because we had cut off the grant in one direction, that we felt justified in coming before this parliament and asking for a very large expenditure to develop allied research work on a scale theretofore never undertaken in Canada by the national research

council which had come into being in the intervening years. We not only asked parliament to give increased votes to the national research council, but we asked for a vote which I think amounts altogether to something like $3,000,000 for the erection in the capital of Canada of the finest industrial research building to be found anywhere. That building will later be still further equipped for scientific research work.
That phase of the work, we thought, the federal parliament should engage upon. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice, speaking the other day, said quite truly:
Technical education has become associated rather with work of a scientific or investigational nature and work of university grade.
It was with regard to technical education that this commission was appointed; it was with regard to technical education that the grants were being made by parliament. And, as my hon. friend has said, technical education is now being associated rather with work of a technical nature and work of university grade. That is exactly the class of work done under the national research council; it is work of that kind that is being carried on in the laboratories here. So that, instead of impeding the work on technical education, the late Liberal administration did more to advance technical education in Canada than had been accomplished by all previous efforts put together. Not only was this building erected as I have said, but additional appropriations were made for research purposes.
I have in my hand the Research Council Act passed on August 27, 1917. This act had not been passed at the time the royal commission of inquiry into technical education was appointed; it was some seven years later. Under this act a new body was formed under which industrial research was to be carried on by a federal advisory council for scientific and industrial research under the control of a committee of the privy council on scientific and industrial research. Let me read a paragraph of the act which deals with the duties of this council. Section 6 reads as follows:
The council shall have charge of all matters affecting scientific and industrial research in Canada which may be assigned to it by the committee, and shall also nave the duty of advising the committee on questions of scientific and technological methods affecting the expansion of Canadian industries or the utilization of the natural resources of Canada.
That is precisely the work described by the Minister of Justice as constituting technical education, namely, work of scientific or investigational nature and of university grade.

Vocational Education
Section 10 which covers the powers of the council reads as follows:
Without thereby limiting the general powers of the council conferred upon or vested in it by this act, it is hereby declared that the council may exercise the following powers, namely:-
(c) To undertake in such way as may be deemed advisable-
(i)	to promote the utilization of the natural
resources of Canada.
(ii)	researches with the object of improving the technical processes and methods used in the industries of Canada, and of discovering processes and methods which may promote the expansion of existing or the development of new industries,
(vi)	the investigation and standardization, at the request of any of the industries of Canada, of the materials which are or may be used in, or of the products of, the industries making such a request,
(vii)	researches, the object of which is to improve conditions in agriculture;
(g) Subject to the approval of the chairman, to publish, from time to time, such scientific and technical information as the council may deem necessary.
Subsection 2 of section 11 reads as follows:
The council, with the approval of the governor in council, may pay to its technical -officers and to others working under its auspices who have made valuable discoveries, inventions or improvements in processes, apparatus and machines such bonuses or royalties as in its opinion may be warranted.
Here we have a statute of Canada, now known as the Research Council Act, 1924, which makes provision for the federal government going into the whole work of technical research -and investigation on a scale never before contemplated. In discontinuing the grants to the provinces the Liberal government had in mind the increase of the work to be carried on by this industrial research council. What has been done in that regard is best shown by a reference to the estimates which this house has been considering this year. In the estimates of this year for the Department of Trade and Commerce, there appears on page 71, an item of $500,000 to cover the work of this research council. Last year there was an item of $500,000, making $1,000,000 in two years. This money was not being expended prior to 1917, nor was it being expended at the time a previous administration made the grants in aid of technical education to the provinces for a period of ten years. We are now committed to an annual expenditure of at least half a million dollars to carry on research work right here in the capital. As I pointed out the other day, the estimates of the Public Works department show an item of $2,000,000 for laboratories and equipment for the
national research council, while in the previous year an amount of $1,541,330 was voted for this purpose. Taking all amounts, within the last two years we 'have spent between four and five million dollars on scientific and industrial research. When the estimates were before the committee the other evening the minister was asked whether or not scholarships could be granted in the universities to promising students to enable them to engage in industrial and scientific research, and the minister replied that that was what was being done under this very act. At the present time this parliament is voting money for scholarships for industrial and scientific research and making payments out of federal funds for the training of young men and women in colleges and universities. However, we are controlling our own expenditures; we are using them in connection with our own sphere of work.
When the estimates of the Department of Mines were being considered the minister asked for something like $750,000 for research work. I asked the minister if that work was all in the nature of industrial research and technical work and he replied that it was. I drew attention to the fact that here again the federal government was expending large sums of money for the purposes of technical education and industrial research.
It has not been with any desire to restrict industrial training or technical education that I have questioned the wisdom of continuing these grants. The truth is quite the opposite. I see the extreme necessity of our own federal government raising increasingly large sums of money for work in the federal sphere. I am anxious that that work shall be carried on in as large a way as may be possible. It cannot be so carried on unless we have the necessary funds, and funds are becoming more and more difficult to provide.
There is another point, one which I have mentioned at different times. It is not wise from the point of view of principle for one government to raise taxes and pass them over to other governments to be expended. The government which raises the taxes ought to control their expenditure. I believe that was the principle laid down at the time of confederation. It was recognized that the provinces would need something in the way of subsidies to supplement their sources of income, but I contend that one of the bases of the confederation act was the idea that the federal and provincial governments would have certain definite fields of services assigned to them, that they should have complete control
Vocational Education

over those services, that they would raise the moneys necessary and see to their expenditure. If for any reason the division is not fair, then adjustments should be made by the paying of additional or altered subsidies.
I have no objection to any just increase which might result from proper revision of the subsidies, but I would point out to my hon. friend that before having the country go further into debt, before imposing more in the way of taxation upon the people, it would be advisable for the government to call a dominion-provincial conference and review the different services which are being carried on by the different administrations, take into account all grants which have been made in the past and are now being made to the provinces by the federal administration and see if it is not possible to make some definite arrangement Whereby the provinces on their part and the Dominion on its part will themselves thereafter raise all that is necessary for the carrying out of the particular services which may be assigned to them. If the provinces have not a sufficient latitude in the way of fields of taxation, then more latitude should be given. I think it will be found with respect to taxation that the provinces have been finding new avenues for raising revenue at a time when the federal government, although it has been making much larger expenditures, is finding it increasingly difficult to obtain revenue. For example, the provinces derive a large revenue from the control of the liquor traffic; they derive large revenues from the licensing of motors and the like; they derive revenues from other sources which were not thought of at the time of confederation.

Mr. Speaker, one of the difficulties that one has to contend with in parliamentary government is that frequently he finds leaders of parties relying upon the statements of their opponents when they were in opposition for the purpose of justifying the action which they now take. Now, either my right hon. friend apposite was right a few years ago when he contended that parliament was following the correct course in permitting grants to be made payable beyond the term of the parliament which was making them, or he was not. He convinced at least a majority of the House of Commons of that day that he was right, and the majority of the House of Commons so decided. It therefore follows that at that particular time at least the party to the left of the Speaker was wrong, and the party to his right was correct in the view which it took.
This afternoon the right hon. gentleman relied upon certain statements made by myself when in opposition as to the unsoundness of making grants of money that extended beyond the life of the parliament that was making them. He referred to my observations on the Old Age Pensions Bill when it was being considered by parliament. He also referred to certain observations I made in connection with the Technical Education

Vocational Education
Act and the Canada Highways Act. But I observed as he read, as doubtless the house did, that I said "except in very extraordinary circumstances or conditions." Now when this bill was considered by the government it was realized that something should be done for technical education by the federal authorities, and as education is primarily a matter for consideration by the provinces it was felt that we would do well to follow the course adopted in 1919. In that year parliament appropriated a very large sum of money, amounting in the aggregate to $10,000,000, for the purposes of technical education.
Now, I submit to this house that technical education is a matter in which the Dominion has a very great interest and a very great stake. Apart altogether from trade and commerce and all that is implied in that, it also has an interest in technical education as distinguished from the narrower interest of the provinces to deal with education as such. We have the interest of the nation, a concern in the ability of our people to meet competition and to carry our wares, our goods, our merchandise successfully into every part of the world. Believing that, we determined, after the commission made a report many years ago, to make an annual grant. This year, however, confronted with extraordinary economic conditions, instead of making a lump sum grant, or a grant which would expire with the life of this parliament, we realized that we must cut our garment according to our cloth-to use an old saying-and therefore we have appropriated a smaller sum of $750,000 to be granted annually for the next fifteen years. It is true that that period of time is far beyond the life of this parliament. It well may be-although there are no indications that warrant such a conclusion just now- beyond the lifetime of the present party in office as a government. But, as I say, there is no likelihood of that being so judging from present appearances.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few brief observations on this bill. If the federal government is in a position financially to make grants to the provinces I do not think it should tie any strings to those grants. If a member on this side of the house ventures to criticize this measure the impression is conveyed to the country by some members on the opposite side that we are against technical education
*1106
Vocational Education

As far as I am concerned, I am not against technical education. But I think the most important part of education to-day, especially under the conditions now prevailing, is primary education. I am going to confine my remarks mainly to Manitoba, because I am more familiar with matters concerning education in that province than with such matters in the other provinces.
In Manitoba, primary education is supported by the municipalities. We have a law under which the municipal authorities contribute S3.60 for every school day in the year -two hundred days-for every school teacher in the municipality, or an annual contribution of S720. Under present economic conditions in western Canada I do not know how we are going to keep our primary schools open. I am not trying to exaggerate the economic conditions, but judging from the latest reports I have-and I think every member from western Canada has been similarly advised-* taxes are not being paid. This being the case, where are we going to find money to keep our primary schools open? Under this proposed legislation we are forcing the provinces to come to an agreement with the federal government in regard to expenditures for technical education. When the federal government votes certain grants to the provinces for education the provinces make every effort possible to comply with the conditions surrounding such grants. It will be so under this bill. What benefit is a child going to get from technical education if he is not able to receive a primary education? In the rural parts of Canada how many of our children take advantage of technical education? Very few of them I venture to say. The reason is that very few pass the higher grades in our primary schools to enable them to take advantage of technical education. If the federal government is in a position to grant moneys to the provinces for educational purposes, let the provinces administer the grants for the benefit of all those under their jurisdiction. I repeat, I am opposed to this proposed legislation-I am not opposed to technical education when it is possible, but I am opposed to this bill because it ties the hands of the provinces-forces them to make certain expenditures which under present conditions they can ill afford to make.
Mr. .D. B. PLUNKETT (Victoria):	Mr. Speaker, I desire to say a word or two on vocational training, because to my mind it concerns the city which I represent and many other cities throughout Canada. Sometimes I think, in legislating for dominion affairs, we altogether forget the provincial side of the

question, so to-night I am going to lay before this house some foots in regard to the tremendous cost entailed to the government of British Columbia in social legislation for which they must tax the people.
In the social legislation of this country I think there are many departments which might well be condensed and a saving made, and I am going to enumerate some of those which affect British Columbia, my own province. Social legislation in British Columbia is becoming more expensive each year, and the burden of taxation has become extremely heavy. Social legislation in British Columbia comes under several headings, and I should like hon. members to listen to this list, because they may be surprised to know that a provincial government should have to carry such a load. Here is the list: conduct of the Labour department; mothers' pensions; old age pensions; home for incurables; charitable institutions; the aid of the destitute; the burial of indigent persons; Tranquil sanatorium for tuberculosis patients; superannuation; health; provincial home; grants to hospitals; the Infants' Act; care of the poor and sick; mental hospitals; industrial schools and unemployment and destitutional relief. That may seem a startling list, and perhaps British Columbia is a little ahead of some of the other provinces in social legislation; as a matter of fact I think it is the leading province in Canada.
What does this mean to the people who have to bear the burden? It will be admitted by every hon. member of this house that federal taxation is a little more indirect than provincial taxation, so the people of the provinces feel this provincial taxation far more than they feel the federal taxation. In the year 1916-17 grants by the province of British Columbia to provide for this work totalled $963,049.03; in 1922-23 the total was $2,447,666; in 1928-29 the amount had increased to $4,099,654.84, while the estimates passed by the British Columbia provincial legislature at the recent session for 1931-32, for those services, totalled $4,466,515.35. It will be seen that the increase from 1916 to 1931 amounts to over $3,500,000.
With regard to education the amount provided by the department in 1916-17, exclusive of the amounts provided by the municipalities, was $1,806,311.76, while last year the vote for education amounted to $4,787,912 or an increase between the years mentioned of over $2,981,600. In passing I might recall to the minds of hon. members that the population of British Columbia is about equal to that of the city of Toronto, while I believe it is the second or third largest province in

Vocational Education
Canada in area. We have a tremendous difficulty in carrying on educational work in the mountainous districts where the lumber interests are centered, and this entails an added expense to the Department of Education in providing schools for those districts; some of them may be only temporary, but they must be provided for the children.
We must look at this measure in two ways. If we are going to have trained mechanics in order to compete in the commerce of the world we must have training schools in which they may obtain a knowledge of their business. It is no use trying to build up an export trade in manufactured goods if we do not build up the knowledge of our citizens in order to produce those goods. I quite agree with what the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) said to-day with regard to the money voted for the national research council; I believe he mentioned two years in each of which $500,000 was voted. But I would ask this question. What good is that national research council to the citizens of my city or to the citizens of Prince Rupert if there should be a young man who wants to learn a trade and acquire technical knowledge at the same time? Is it not necessary to have some of these schools in the larger cities? Unfortunately it is true that a technical school is the most costly of all our institutions of this kind; the machinery and equipment require a great deal of money, and I think the government might go further and give some allowance to the provinces to help maintain these schools after they are established.
I commend the action of the government in this regard; I think money could not be spent in a better way., Some time there will come a readjustment of the taxation system of this country, and our taxes will be rearranged as between the province and the Dominion. At the present time I feel that the provinces have too heavy a burden, and therefore I am pleased to support the action of this government in voting money for this purpose.

It was my honour and privilege for a time to be president of the school trustees' association of Manitoba, and on one occasion I chose . vocational training as the theme of a presidential address. Undoubtedly in the past our school curricula have tended more to produce professional men than men who will take part in the ordinary business of life. Perhaps two years ago I would not have had the slightest hesitation in heartily endorsing this bill, even though there may be involved such constitutional questions as jurisdiction and the rights of the provinces and the Dominion.
I have not usually attached undue importance to these questions. But according to the reports that come to us from the west, those provinces-I know this for a fact-not only this year but for some years to come will find it very difficult indeed to support the primary schools. There can be no question about that. Someone foolishly made the statement the other day in a newspaper interview that one good crop would bring Saskatchewan back. That is absolute folly. Debts have been piling up during the last two or three years and obligations have been incurred from which the provinces, either as governments or as individuals, will be unalble to escape for many years. In the face of this fact it seems to me that it would be well for us to go slowly. I believe in vocational training with all my heart, but as things are in our western provinces I believe the government would be wise not to ask the provinces just now to assume obligations which they will not be able to discharge. It is quite possible that Ontario and Quebec, these central wealthy provinces, will be able to fulfil the conditions imposed by this bill. I am quite satisfied that the prairie provinces will not be able to take advantage of the opportunities here offered for technical education, and possibly what is true of those provinces is true also to some extent of the maritimes. Of the maritime provinces, however, I cannot speak. That is my attitude to this bill; not one of opposition

Vocational Education

but a firm conviction that under the present circumstances it woudl be well for the government not to pass this legislation inviting the provinces to take on responsibilities which I am sure they will not be in a position to bear.

subtopic: PROPOSED ANNUAL EXPENDITURE OF $750,000 CONDITIONAL UPON AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext: In Saskatchewan we have already assumed all these obligations; we have spent hundreds of thousands of dollars in the building of technical schools. Does my hon. friend want to drop all this? Does he want us to abandon all that we have done, or shall we continue?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

I have just a word to say at this point in the debate. The questions asked by my hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) and by my hon. friend from Lisgar (Mr. Brown) I should prefer to discuss when the bill is in committee; we shall have wider scope then.
I do not know that I should have risen to say anything now had it not been for the speech of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) this afternoon, when he tried to take me to task for certain statements I have made in this house at various times with reference to his own record upon technical education. I do not want to quibble with my right hon. friend as to whether I mentioned the "first occasion" or the "second occasion" when I spoke upon the introduction of the bill. I realize that the first occasion on which the question was brought to the attention of this parliament, and by myself, was in 1907. My right hon. friend was not then a member of the House of Commons and therefore I could not have made any reference to him in regard to that first occasion in 1907.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROPOSED ANNUAL EXPENDITURE OF $750,000 CONDITIONAL UPON AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext: My hon. friend's words were that I killed his first resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSED ANNUAL EXPENDITURE OF $750,000 CONDITIONAL UPON AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
There is the quibble on
the word "first." I meant the first time I moved the resolution, when the right hon. gentleman was present. Is that clear? I am not referring to the occasion two years previously, before he was a member. Let us fix the occasion definitely, whether you call it first or second: It was in December, 1909. My right hon. friend was Minister of Labour; I was a humble member supporting the Liberal party and the government of which he was a member. And at the instance of very important bodies in this country, notably the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, and various similar organizations, I brought forward a resolution for the appointment of a
IMr. Brown.]
commission to inquire into questions relating to technical education. The right hon. gentleman, as Minister of Labour, discussed my motion in an elaborate and very interesting speech. The whole temper of the house was distinctly in favour of my resolution, but unfortunately for it my right hott. friend saw fit to move the adjournment of my motion, though he knew, as I knew, and every other member in the house knew, that should his motion of adjournment carry my motion would be relegated to the foot of the list. And under the rules of the house in those days my motion would not be reached again. He knew that; the whole house knew it. When he moved the adjournment of my motion the opposition of the day immediately challenged him upon the ground that he was trying to sidetrack the whole question-that was the word used in the debate. It was assumed by the opposition, of course, that the move of my right hon. friend as Minister of Labour was for the purpose of killing my motion, or postponing it, or, as was said on that occasion, sidetracking it. That was why Mr. Fielding got up and explained that the government did not intend to sidetrack it: he knew what the house believed. Well, the matter was put to the vote, the majority prevailed, and my right hon. friend's motion to kill my motion carried. And on that occasion I voted for the first time with the Conservative party. That vote constitutes one important milestone in my career.
My motion having been adjourned, or abandoned, or sidetracked, whichever way my right hon. friend wishes me to refer to it, considerable agitation arose throughout Canada among the parties interested; and if my right hon. friend will turn up the Toronto Globe of the day following he will see how strong was the protestation against the abandonment of the matter. At any rate, as I remember well, after the Christmas adjournment I was one of a deputation that waited upon Sir Wilfrid Laurier. In that deputation, I think, were Mr. Draper of Ottawa, Mr. O'Donoghue of Toronto, Mr. James Simpson of Toronto, a gentleman from my own riding and myself, and we urged upon the Prime Minister that the matter should not be dropped. These people were serious; they insisted that a commission should be appointed. Later on in that spring the then Minister of Labour, now leader of the opposition, did communicate, as he says, with the various provinces and did appoint a commission. The appointment was made in June 1910. Then ended the first step in the matter.

Vocational Education
My right hon. friend in the speech which he made on my motion expressed the warmest sympathy with the subject of technical education.

What the men who were earnest and interested in this matter wanted was not sympathy, but action, and the only action taken, and that under a certain amount of pressure, was when in June the commission was appointed.
When the commission made its report, a long and very interesting one, the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier was out of office and the government of Sir Robert Borden was in office. No further practical step was taken in the matter until 1919. The war intervened. I was a member of the government in 1919 but I do not think my right hon. friend was a member of the house at that time. The government of that day brought in a bill to grant $1,000,000 per year for ten years to the various provinces in aid of technical education. It is interesting to note that the late hon. Mr. Fielding was in the house in 1919. I believe I placed on record the statement which he made in the house in the session of 1919 in regard to the bill, but I will mention it again just to emphasize what Mr. Fielding said. The following appears on page 3796 of Hansard of June 20, 1919:
As regards technical education, it is worth remembering that this grant, although it is late in coming, is the outcome of a policy which the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier took up some years ago.
The money grant by this parliament was the outcome of the policy of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, in whose government my right hon. friend was Minister of Labour. The grant of 1919 was the outcome of the policy of the government in which my right hon. friend sat. Mr. Fielding also said:
When the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier appointed that commission, headed by Professor Robertson and including a number of able men,
22110-261}
we certainly created the impression that in some degree the matter was a dominion one, and I look upon this movement as a belated endeavour on the part of the government to carry out the intentions which the Liberal government had in mind when they appointed that commission.
That is a very clear and distinct statement from an able and prominent member of the Liberal administration, the late Bon. Mr. Fielding. When the bill passed the house in 1919 I do not think my right hon. friend was in the house. No further action wa3 taken until 19129 when my right hon. friend was Prime Minister of Canada. The matter came up again at the instance of the opposition. The ten years period had expired, some of the provinces had received almost their whole allotment of money while other provinces had a considerable balance yet to be received. The question was: would the grants lapse or would they be continued? When the matter was brought to the attention of the house on that occasion, my right hon. friend used the following language:
There was no thought at the outset that the federal government would be called upon to go further than simply to supply the information to the provinces which would enable them to develop their educational systems along lines of industrial training and technical education.
My right hon. friend stated there was no thought that the government should do more than gather information. Mr. Fielding stated that the grant of 1919 was the outcome of a Laurier policy. I think Mr. Fielding was correct notwithstanding the statements made in this house in 1929 by my right hon. friend, as I have just quoted them.

In the past the wishes of the various provinces have been met in this respect. Letters have, been received during the present year,1 bin at the meeting that was convened in Ottawa by the government of my right hon. friend in 1927, all the provinces were represented and all the resolutions passed there were tcu the same effect, commending the system as' inaugurated by the government of the Dominion of Canada, commending the operation of the plan in the various provinces and asking for renewals of the grants.
