Take, for instance, towns like Ken ora or Fort Frances; they are probably three hundred miles away from a large city, yet they are the centre of a large and important section of the country. The young men and the young women from that part of the country would of necessity have to travel as far as Fort William in order to obtain the benefit of technical education. I was wondering if the minister would not think it advisable to make provision in the agreements to be entered into with the provinces to assist those distant localities to a greater extent, so that the benefits of technical -education will not all be concentrated in large cities like Fort William, Winnipeg, Toronto ;and Montreal. I think the point raised by my hon. friend from Bonaventure is very well taken. It is one that I was going to suggest to the minister, and I commend it tp him because the people in the distant rural parts -this is the least important factor-are paying their share of the cost of technical education through taxation, yet they are unable to secure any of the benefits of it because of the fact that they live in scattered rural districts, where taxation is already very high. Kenora, with a population of 8,000 thought of establishing a 'technical school, but when the Ontario government sent their inspector up there to inquire into the situation, they determined that the school would hardly fit in with the taxation of the town and everything else connected with it. I would suggest to the minister that it might be well to take into consideration ways and means of assisting these localities through the agreements. As the agreements read at the present time-I have a copy of them here-we have very little to say except in the matetr of assisting the provinces with a grant. They themselves determine where the technical schools shall be established, and they spend the grant that we give them.

speechtext: Saskatchewan has an unexpended balance of $436,000 over a period of eleven years, Manitoba an unexpended balance of $448,000 over a period of eleven years, and Nova Scotia, which the Minister of Fisheries said was taking such advantage of the grants and desired to have them continued, has an unexpended balance of $267,000 over a period of eleven years. There is proof positive that those three provinces at least are not so very anxious that these amounts be voted to them, because they have not been taking advantage of the amounts hitherto available. Here we have over $1,000,000 in three provinces unexpended after eleven years' operation of the act, and in order to give them further time to take'advantage of the grant we had in 1929 to extend for a further five years the term during which the unexpended balance might be spent. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROPOSED ANNUAL EXPENDITURE OF $750,000 CONDITIONAL UPON AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on tlie second reading of the bill my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) in closing the debate, said he would not have spoken but for the remarks of the leader of the opposition. May I say that I had no intention of speaking on the third reading, but I am doing so now in virtue of the speech made by the Minister of Justice.
In his speech my hon. friend repeated what he had previously said anti what after the quotations I gave this afternoon from his own speeches I thought perhaps he would correct when he came to speak to-night. His statement was to the effect that I had been responsible for killing his motion at the time it was introduced. I think even to my hon. friend himself it is now quite clear that his first motion was killed by himself; for in the speech he made in the house on a subsequent occasion with regard to it he said that his own words had not been effective. enough to convince the house. But with regard to the second motion, so that there may be no possibility of any quibbling about the matter, my hon. friend said that unfortunately my motion, as Minister of Labour, was made to kill his motion. In other words, he repeated what he previously said, that in 1909 when I moved the adjournment of the debate it was to kill his motion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSED ANNUAL EXPENDITURE OF $750,000 CONDITIONAL UPON AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext: It had that effect.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROPOSED ANNUAL EXPENDITURE OF $750,000 CONDITIONAL UPON AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
I said this
afternoon that my purpose in moving the adjournment of the debate was to enable the government to make progress in appointing a commission, and that the whole purpose was to get the consent of the governments of the provinces so that there would be no question of jurisdiction raised to embarrass the work of the commission, and to get the commission appointed at the earliest possible date. Now I wish to repeat what my hon. friend then said with respect to my motion for adjournment, in order to show what -was his view at that time, and I would ask the committee to judge for themselves whether these words sound as though my motion, in his estimation, was killing his motion. I refer to page 1096 of Hansard for December 6, 1909:
As mover of the resolution I may say a word on the motion to adjourn. After dealing with the question somewhat fully this afternoon, and endeavouring to impress upon the government the propriety of the motion, and also the expediency of appointing a commission forthwith, I hardly think it would be consistent for me now to vote for the postponement of my own motion. However, I accept in absolute
good faith the statement made by the Minister of Labour in asking for an adjournment of this debate in order to give the government further time to consider the question. If I thought there was the slightest foundation for the statement of the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Reid) ....
Who, by the way, had said that the motion was in order to sidetrack the whole matter. Then my hon. friend goes on to say:
.... I would be the more inclined to press the matter with all the resources at my command. But I accept the statement of my hon. friend the Minister of Labour, and the positive assurance given to this house by the Minister of Finance that the government does feel in sympathy with the main purpose of this resolution, but requires further time for consideration.
Then a little later on he said:
However, as I feel satisfied that the government has evidently the intention of going ahead on this matter and desires only time for consideration, I do not ask anyone to support what may be my vote if a division is taken.
Those are my hon. friend's words in reference to two persons, myself, and the late Right Hon. W. S. Fielding, who is no longer here to speak for himself. I propose to say a word on my own behalf, and I also propose to say a word with respect to the late Right Hon. Mr. Fielding, who is no longer in this parliament to answer my hon. friend. With regard to myself, and to show that my motion was simply to enable the government of the day to get some information that we might proceed with the speedy appointment of a commission, my hon. friend said:
However, I accept in absolute good faith the statement made by the Minister of Labour in asking for an adjournment of this debate in order to give the government further time to consider the question.
When my hon. friend said he accepted my w-ord in absolute good faith he was speaking as one gentleman to another, in the presence of gentlemen in the House of Commons. He was doing more than that; he was then, as he described himself this evening, a humble member of parliament speaking to a minister of the 'crown. To-day he is speaking as a minister of the crown to a humble member of the opposition, and what my hon. friend in 1909 said he was prepared to accept in good faith as a gentleman, and as a member of the House of Commons, to-day as a minister of the crown he says is a matter of bad faith. I am sorry for the changes the years have brought in the attitude of my hon. friend. I thought the present Minister of Justice was a man of his word; I thought that the present Minister of Justice, when he said to anyone, "I will accept your statement in good faith", would, so long as he
Vocational Education

lived, remain true to his word. I can only regret that hereafter I shall not be able to feel that, when Minister of Justice in the government of another party, he was as true to his word as he was when a humble member of the. Liberal party.
May I say a word on behalf of the Right Hon. Mr. Fielding? The present Minister of Justice has brought into this debate the name of a gentleman than which none is more honoured in the parliament of Canada. The hon. member has cited Mr. Fielding because of his known integrity, because of the type of man he was, a gentleman whose word he knew would weigh with all hon. members of this House of Commons. This evening he has given to the house, from the speech made by Mr. Fielding in 1909, certain citations which he says confirm the view that my motion made in that year was intended to kill his and that what was being done by the government in 1919 was in furtherance of the original intention of the Laurier administration, and that this original intention was not to gather information as I have said. Let me read what the Right Hon. Mr. Fielding said, and let me lend to his words the added emphasis of one who is not here to speak for himself but whose name is revered even by the present Minister 'of Justice. This is what Mr. Fielding said, as reported in Hansard of December 6, page 1089:
I must take exception entirely to the observation of an hon. gentleman opposite, that the motion to adjourn is a motion to side-track this resolution.
That was what Mr. Fielding said regarding the comment that had been made by Doctor Reid, who was member for Grenville, that the motion was to sidetrack the resolution. The Minister of Justice tried to convey to the house to-night the impression that in Mr. Fielding's opinion there was an attempt through my motion to sidetrack the resolution, and these are the words of Mr. Fielding:
I must take exception entirely to the observation of an hon. gentleman opposite, that the motion to adjourn is a motion to side-track this resolution; and while I propose to vote for the motion to adjourn, I do so on altogether a different ground. After the discussion we have had. after the abundance of information brought before the house, showing the great need of this movement in Canada, it would indeed be strange if nothing further should be done. We are 'all of the opinion that something should be done, and the only question is what is the better way of doing it.
Then further on:
I am going to vote for the adjournment of the debate, not for the purpose of sidetracking

the matter, but that we may have further opportunity of considering, not the wisdom of doing something, but the best way in which to do it.
And finally:
I do so in order that we may have the opportunity of considering further' what is the best way to aid a movement which seems to have received the favour of the whole house.
I do not believe there is a single member who will not accept, verbatim et literatim, every word uttered by the late Mr. Fielding at that time. I could wish for the Minister of Justice that when he has passed away, and when his words are being quoted in this parliament in years to come, they might be received as unreservedly as the words of Mr. Fielding have been accepted by himself.
I was a little over generous when I said a moment ago to my hon. friend that the letter which I sent out immediately after the debate in question was dated December 30. I find fiat the letter was sent on December 13, the 30th being the date of one of the replies. That was not as he said a year or so after my hon. friend's motion was voted down. My hon. friend made his speech in the House of Commons on December 6. He knows, as hon. gentlemen do, all that is involved in departmental correspondence, the preparation of communications, and so on. I ask whether much time was lost in carrying out the promise of the then administration given by myself as Minister of Labour to take steps immediately to appoint a commission. That promise was made on December 6, 1909, and on December 13, 1909, the following letter was sent to each of the premiers of the different provinces:
Department of Labour, Canada.
Ottawa, December 13, 1909. Dear Sir:	_	...
The Dominion government is considering the advisability of appointing a royal commission to inquire into the needs and present equipment of the Dominion as respects industrial training and technical education, and into the systems and methods of technical instruction _ obtaining in other countries, particularly in Great Britain, France, Germany and the _ United States. It is intended that the commission shall he solely for the purpose of gathering information, the information when obtained to be published in a suitable report to be at the disposal of the provinces and available for general distribution.
I may say that the view of the government is that a commission of the kind suggested might render valuable services to the _ Dominion as a whole, since it would be m a position to conduct an inquiry on a wider and more comprehensive scale than might be considered desirable or possible in _ the ease of the different provinces, and which if undertaken by the provinces individually must lead inevitably to the duplication and reduplication of energy and expense.

Vocational Education
It is recognized, however, that the work of such a commission, to be of national service, should have the hearty endorsation of the governments of the several provinces of the Dominion, and I am. therefore, writing to ask if the appointment by the federal authorities of a commission of the character and scope suggested would meet with the approval of your government, and to inquire, in particular, inasmuch as some doubt has bean expressed on the point, whether exception to such a course would be taken on any ground of jurisdiction.
Yours faithfully,
W. L. Mackenzie King.
Then the replies came from the different premiers. I read some of them this afternoon, but inasmuch as my hon. friend this evening sought to have the committee believe that I was stating something that was not correct, when I said that the original purpose of the commission was solely that of gathering information, that tha.t was the ground on which the commission was appointed, let me read again a paragraph or two from some of the replies. Here is a communication from Sir James Whitney:
Office of the Prime Minister and President of the Council, Ontario
Toronto, December 16, 1909. Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King,
Minister of Labour,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir:
I have your letter of the 13th instant.
I understand the object of the proposed commission, to inquire into the needs and present equipment of the Dominion as respects training and technical education and into the system of methods for technical instruction obtaining in other countries, will be solely for the purpose of gathering information. This being so, I see no objection to the creation of the commission, and no exception will be taken to it on the part of the province of Ontario.
Yours very truly,
J. P. Whitney.
I will give one other letter-reference to others will be found in the speech I made this afternon on the second reading. This letter is from the premier of the province of Quebec. It will be seen that I have taken the two largest and most important provinces.
Office of tlie Prime Minister, Province of Quebec
Quebec, December- 30, 1909. Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King,
Minister of Labour,
Ottawa, Ont.
Sir:
I have submitted to my colleagues of the executive council the letter you were kind enough to write to me on the 13th inst., asking me whether the government of the province of Quebec would approve the appointment by the federal authorities of a commission to make an
investigation concerning technical instruction in this country.
We are of the opinion, my colleagues and myself, that anything pertaining to public education-whether the subject be special teaching or general teaching-belongs to the provinces exclusively, and I want to write you so, in order that there may be no misunderstanding on that point. As, on the other hand, you give me the assurance that the federal authorities, in instituting a commission of investigation, would simply do it with a view to help the provincial governments, by having collected information which they would later on put at the disposal of the latter, we see no objection to the appointment of such a commission.
Please accept, sir, the expression of my highest regard.
Lomer Gouin,
Prime Minister.
These letters I have quoted will show the reason for my repeated statement that the original intention in appointing the commission was solely that it should gather information to be placed at the disposal of the provinces, so that there should be no question of invasion by the Dominion of provincial jurisdiction in the matter of education. Having been responsible for the appointment of the commission, I have ever since felt responsible to the provinces for maintaining the position which I then took. I have before me a copy of the order in council which covered the appointment of the commission. It reads:
Certified copy of a report of the committee of the privy council approved by His Excellency the Governor General on the 1st June, 1910.
Let me direct attention to the date of that recommendation. As hon. members know, while parliament is in session ministers find it very difficult to arrange the personnel of commissions and the like. The last replies received from the different provinces came in around January or February, and in May of the same year, as Minister of Labour I made my recommendation to the cabinet for the appointment of the commission. The order in council reads as follows:

That is the story. On December 6, the government of the day promised that it would take immediate steps to appoint a commission, but it desired first to communicate with the premiers of the different provinces to make sure that no question of jurisdiction would be raised. On December 13, 1909, communications were sent to the premiers of the provinces and replies were received during the balance of that year and extending into the next. One was dated Victoria, January 15, which would reach Ottawa the latter part of the month. On March 13, 1910, an amount appeared in the supplementary estimates for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1910, as an appropriation for the commission. That amount was not included in the estimates for the following year but in the supplementary estimates for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1910. This was done so that the commission could ibe speedily appointed. The recommendation to the council was made by the Minister of Labour on May 28, 1910, and the authority for the appointment was dated June 1, 1910.
The commission then started on its duties and visited different parts of this country.

Vocational Education
It made several interim reports but it was not until 1913 that the final report came in. My hon. friend has said that they acted on the final report the next year, but let me read what the commission said.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSED ANNUAL EXPENDITURE OF $750,000 CONDITIONAL UPON AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext: I said that the government of which I was a member took action in 1919.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROPOSED ANNUAL EXPENDITURE OF $750,000 CONDITIONAL UPON AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
In 1919 the
government took action upon the report which had been brought in in 1913. Let me read one paragraph of the report, as follows:
The commission recommends that the sum of $3,000,000 be provided annually for a period of ten years by the parliament of Canada and paid annually into a Dominion development fund.
Did the government of the day aot on that recommendation? Instead of acting on it and making an annual grant of $3,000,000 for ten years, it passed an act to provide for the annual payment of $1,000,000 spread over a period of ten years. It gave less than one-third of the amount suggested by the commission as being necessary as a development fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSED ANNUAL EXPENDITURE OF $750,000 CONDITIONAL UPON AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext: My hon. friend must not forget that a war had occurred in the meantime.

subtopic: PROPOSED ANNUAL EXPENDITURE OF $750,000 CONDITIONAL UPON AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
There was a
war in the meantime and ever since this country has been endeavouring to pay for that war but has not succeeded. While that war was proceeding every dollar of the finances required on war account was money borrowed by the government then in office, and it was left to subsequent governments to meet the expenses. We have to-day a condition in this country which, considered from the point of view of its possible effect upon trade and industry, is almost as serious as periods of war have been in different countries at different times. We have at the present time a condition in Canada to meet which the Prime Minister intends to announce to-morrow night, I do not know what measure of relief. I shall be very much surprised if this parliament is not asked to vote some such sum as $50,000,000, $75,000,000 or $100,000,000 to relieve the present situation. Many men and women have no work, they have no food to eat, some no clothing to wear, and are unable to pay their bills. Is this a time for the government to be asking the people to spend additional amounts of money in grants to the provinces, when, as has been pointed out to-night, some of the provinces have not been able to use the total amount of grants that have been
made to them; when in addition to that, municipality after municipality has been communicating to the provinces its inability to carry the burden resulting from the provinces passing on to the municipalities the raising of amounts equivalent to some of the grants which the Dominion has furnished for certain purposes? I am as strongly in favour of promoting technical education and vocational training and I have done as much in regard to getting industrial training developed as any other man in the country. I was responsible for the appointment of the commission the report of which lies at the basis of this whole matter. I was the one who brought into parliament the recommendation for the appointment of a commission to study the question of technical education when the present Minister of Justice says himself that he could not have his voice heard in the matter of getting support for his proposals. This commission made its report and my hon. friend tells us to-night that on the basis of this report the governments of the day have since acted. Yet he would seek to deny the administration of which I was a member any credit for any part in this matter, and particularly in regard to myself he would seek to make out that I had killed his motion, citing in a manner wholly misleading in support of his statement the words of one who is no longer here to speak for himself. I do not wonder hon. gentlemen opposite sigh. After all, there are some things that are befitting even in parliamentary debate.
When this afternoon I spoke on the second reading I pointed out that within the last two years this very parliament of which we are members at the present time will have voted -if we include what is in the estimates today, has already passed the house and will shortly receive His Excellency's assent-the sum of $1,000,000 for industrial research work, which is part of the technical education work of the country, to be given to the industrial research council that was not in existence at the time the technical education act was first passed. May I point out that in addition to that the house will have voted within the past two years something approaching another $3,000,000 for the construction in this very' city of Ottawa of the finest research laboratory on the continent; that this house has voted another $750,000 for further research work in connection with the Department of Mines. According to the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) the other evening the national research council itself has been awarding scholarships to
Vocational Education

young men and women throughout the country to go into the universities, technical colleges and elsewhere in order to qualify as experts in matters of industrial and technical research. I have supported all these measures, and been 'largely responsible for some of them. I have pointed this out to make clear that I am not opposing any aid to industrial and technical education. I have shown that inside two years something like $5,000,000 has been voted for this purpose. This measure calls now in addition for the expenditure of a sum of $750,000 a year for a period of fifteen years.
Surely these are things of which account ought to be taken, and I again appeal to the ministry, although I know my words will not he harkened to, to consider whether the time has not come when we ought to call the provinces into conference to find out, where there is any doubt, what services should be carried on by the provinces, what services should be carried on by the Dominion, what is a fair adjustment of financial arrangements between them, what are the sources of revenue and taxation for each of them to have. If as a result of that conference it is decided that the British North America Act should be amended so that the federal parliament shall take over in its entirety the work of industrial and technical education in all parts of Canada, -1 shall be prepared to support a recommendation of that kind. If, on the other hand, it is decided that the provinces shall do the work of vocational training and that the Dominion government shall do that of higher industrial research work of the type in which the universities are engaged, I shall be prepared to support that. If it is decided that the Dominion should take over tihe old age pensions scheme and administer it in its entirety, I shall support that gladly and I say here and now that is what I think ought to be immediately done. If, further, it is decided with respect to unemployment and other matters there is to be a division whereby the Dominion will assume certain Obligations and the provinces other obligations, I shall be prepared to consider favourably recommendations that are made along those lines.
What I submit, howeveT, is this; whether we have made mistakes in the past-and I was frank enough the other evening to say that with respect to some of those grants I did make the mistake of countenancing contributions to the provinces, but I thought experience had shown that was not wise

if as a result of a conference of that kind, we come to the conclusion that these different grants should not be continued, but that larger subsidies should be given to the

provinces; that the provinces should be allowed certain fields of taxation which are not used by them at the present time, I shall be prepared to consider all these things on their merits. The constitution of this country was framed by men who gave the matter very serious thought, who were very careful in outlining respective spheres of action for the provinces and the Dominion, and who showed, that by making provision for the adjustment of accounts through subsidies,, they felt that any money that went from the federal treasury should go to the provinces to be dealt with by the provinces as they might deem best, -but not that provincial jurisdiction should be invaded by the Dominion nor that the Dominion should seek to put pressure on' the provinces.
The Minister of Justice said the other day that this legislation would give more power to the provinces, and he supported it on that ground. Is not that an extraordinary position for the Minister of Justice of the federal government to take? More power to the provinces where federal finances are involved means less power to the Dominion. The-Minister of Justice is here to maintain the power of the Dominion. One thing which we as members of the federal House of Commons have to safeguard is the rights of the Dominion. In this house many speeches have been made, to which no exception can be taken in any particular, about the needs of provinces and what the provinces should do; but this is the parliament in which to discuss the needs and taxation of the Dominion, and this is -the place where primarily matters of federal and not of provincial obligation must be settled.
May I conclude with this word: I remember very well when in 1916 this parliament was discussing the question whether it w-ould without sanction of the electorate extend the term of parliament for one year, when under the constitution it had not the -authority so to do. I was not a member of parliament at the time, but I was in very close association with the late Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier who honoured me with his confidence in matters -of the kind, and I know something of the discussions which took place. I remember very well Sir WTlfrid Laurier saying at that time: Once wre trifle with the constitution and seek to do things which by the constitution were never intended, we put profane hands upon the ark of the covenant and no one can say how far the resultant injury is likely to extend. That is a very sound doctrine. If the constitution is not right, amend it; make it as it should be; but as

long as we have a constitution setting forth certain powers for the Dominion and certain powers for the provinces, we shall not err very much but will rather be doing our duty as members of the federal parliament if we adhere to that constitution in spirit as well as in letter.

Mr. Chairman, the other night when we were dealing with items 438 and 438a I made a statement to the effect that whenever the minister under the. authority of an order in council-which order in council would be issued under the authority of t)he customs act passed at the special session-placed an arbitrary valuation on goods for duty purposes, the valuation invariably would be above the invoice value, that this always tended to induce the importer to pay a higher price for the goods to the foreign producer than he would otherwise pay, and that if he did not do so the customs department would impose a fine on him in the form of a dumping duty equal to the excess price he might pay. I stated further that the importer because of that condition would always be tempted to pay a foreign manufacturer more than was necessary, thus transferring to the coffers of foreign producers money that otherwise might come into the treasury of the Dominion. I mentioned automobiles. The minister at the time informed me that that could not happen. My purpose in speaking to-night is to show that it can happen, tlhat it does happen, and that it is inevitable that it should happen.
It will be recalled that in 1922 the government of the day passed an amendment to the customs act known as 47a. That amendment gave the minister power to place an arbitrary valuation on natural products coming into the country, which valuation should be the value for duty. That amendment remained a dead letter on the statute books until 1926, when my hon. friends opposite were in power. They enforced the act; they passed an order in council giving the minister power to place this arbitrary valuation ' on certain natural products.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Fruits and vegetables.
Mr. Y'OUNG: Yes, fruits and vegetables. Not only did the minister fix this valuation and thereby increase the duty, but the officials of the department took that arbitrary valuation as a basis for accusing the importer of dumping, and they added the dumping duty. When we discovered that this was being done we protested to the departmental officials. They insisted on their right to charge that dumping duty; we insisted they had no such right, until finally they consented to appeal to the Department of Justice for an opinion. The Department of Justice declared they had no right to impose a dumping duty because of the arbitrary valuation which had been placed on the article. In spite of that they continued for a time to

Customs Tariff

collect that dumping duty until finally an appeal was taken to the governor in council and the orders in council were rescinded.
Matters remained in that state until the September session of the present parliament, when amendments were passed to the Customs Act which gave the minister power to place an arbitrary valuation not only on natural products but on almost anything coming into this country, such valuation to be the value for duty. Those were the amendments to the Customs Act, and having done that an amendment was passed to the customs tariff. That is section 6 of the customs tariff, which was the dumping clause, and I wish to read that section as it was amended last fall:
In the case of articles exported to Canada of a class or kind made or produced in Canada, if the export or actual selling price to an importer in Canada is less than the fair market value of the same article when sold for home consumption in the usual and ordinary course in the country whence exported to Canada at the time of its exportation to Canada, or is less than the fair market value or value for duty thereof as determined under the provisions of section thirty-six of the Customs Act, or is less than the fair market value thereof as fixed by the governor in council under the provisions of section thirty-seven of the Customs Act, or is less than the value for duty thereof as determined by the minister under the provisions of paragraphs (a) and (e) of section forty-one of the Customs Act, or is less than the fair market value thereof as fixed by the minister under the provisions of section forty-three of the Customs Act, there shall, in addition to the duties otherwise established, be levied, collected and paid on such article, on its importation into Canada, a special or dumping duty, equal to the difference between the said selling price of the article for export and the said fair market value thereof or value for duty thereof; and such special or dumping duty shall be levied, collected and paid on such article although it is not otherwise dutiable.
This is the meaning of that amendment: Where the minister has exercised his power of fixing a value for duty on almost any goods-since the power goes that far now- if that value is higher than the price the man actually paid for the goods then the man shall be charged a dumping duty .equal to the difference between the price so fixed by the minister and the price he pays. The other day my contention was that the man was thereby tempted to pay a higher price to the foreign canufacturer, with whom very often he is friendly, rather than pay the dumping duty, and that the effect of this legislation is to force Canadians to pay higher prices to foreign producers than those producers receive from their own people, and higher prices than it is necessary for the Canadian to pay. The minister said such

a thing could not happen, but I have here three letters which I think will convince him that it not only can but does happen. Here is a letter from the Edgerton Manufacturing Company, Plymouth, Indiana, who I believe manufacture baskets for packing fruit. The letter is addressed to the Norfolk Fruit Growers' Association of Simcoe, Ontario, and the paragraph I desire to read is as follows:
You may be interested in knowing that the freight rate on the cars we shipped you during the 1930 season averaged 17-6 cents per dozen packages. This amount added to the price of $1.80 per dozen as fixed by the Dominion government would result in a cost to you of $1-976 per dozen without taking into consideration the duty. The action of the Dominion government would increase your delivered price approximately 25 cents per dozen and, likewise, would result in a profit to us of about 20 cents per dozen higher than that which we enjoy on sales made in the states. We feel that our profit on Canadian business should be approximately the same as that received in connection with business done in the states.
Here is a firm which frankly states that because of the action of the customs department they are compelled to charge Canadians 20 cents a dozen more than they charge Americans for the same goods. I also have a letter from the Western Cartridge Company of East Alton, Illinois, dated May 6, 1931:
On January 3rd this year we reduced ammunition prices to all of our customers in the United States by 10 per cent, and we extended the same discount at the same time to our customers in Canada. The Canadian commissioner of customs has refused to accept this extra discount of 10 per cent on shipments of our goods into Canada, and has threatened to charge dumping duty against our goods so invoiced; and, based on this decision of the commissioner, we have been obliged to withdraw these reduced prices from our Canadian customers and are now invoicing them at a price 10 per cent higher than we charge any of our domestic jobbing trade. This additional 10 per cent is, of course, in the last analysis, paid by the consumer of Western ammunition in the Dominion, and we regard it as distinctly unfair to him and his interests.
We have been told that the commissioner's decision was based on a brief presented to the Dominion government in Ottawa by the Dominion Cartridge Company, in which brief they indicated their reasons for protesting the reduction in price of American-made ammunition. We should like to obtain a copy of this Dominion Cartridge Company brief as presented to the government, in order to be in a position to present, if advisable, our answer to it.
I might say that I asked for a copy of that brief in order that we might find out vhat the cartridge company asked for and whether or not their claims were proper and sound, but the government saw fit not to grant that request.

It is disturbing to find the hon. gentleman so inaccurate. The first case, the Edgerton case, is one in which the goods were being sold at less than cost of production, and the minister had nothing to do with it. It is covered by a statute of this parliament. That statute was not enacted by this government; in the form to which I have directed attention it has existed for many years. When it is suggested that the dumping duty was treated in the manner indicated, I recall that when the Minister of Customs of that day, Mr. Bureau, introduced the legislation in question he indicated that the dumping duty would apply, and it was subsequently discovered, as the hon. gentleman knows, that that was not the case. But inasmuch as it was the intention of parliament that it should, when this government did legislate it legislated to give effect to the intention of parliament as Mr. Bureau had then stated it, and as parliament understood it, although it was opposed by my hon. friends opposite and to the right, and supported by the Conservative party of that day. So that the legislation as it now stands means exactly what the Minister of Customs of that day said it was intended that it should mean, and what it was regarded as meaning. Now keeping that in mind and the fact that the Johnson case-the fruit baskets-is one that oomes within the letter of the law and in which the minister had nothing to do with fixing either values or prices, but which automatically involved the application of the duties to which the hon. gentleman has referred, I think he will agree with me that that passes out of the picture. That is No. 1. No. 2, the cartridge case, considerably intrigued me when I heard my hon. friend refer to it the other day. I took the trouble to investigate it. The truth is that that American cartridge company for whom apparently the gentleman named has 'been so solicitous was selling cartridges in this country at what was represented to be a price less than cost of production.
Mr. Y'OUNG: By whom was it so represented?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
By the manufacturers of cartridges and by others in this country, the merchants who were dealing in Canadian-made products in competition with the American product. The result was that the minister directed an investigation tr be held-not the
Customs Tariff

minister but the administrative 'branch of the Department of National Revenue. I need hardly point out to so well-informed a gentleman as my hon. friend from Weyburn (Mr. Young) that these investigations are being held continuously. Investigations are proceeding every day of the year with respect to this much-vexed question of the prices at which goods are being sold, thereby displacing Canadian goods in our markets. This is nothing new. It is not the caprice of a minister; it is a well-established principle of our customs law. Nor has it been in force only since a new government came into being; it was in force during the long years from 1896 to 1911. In fact, it was during those years that it developed, because during the years of the war very little attention was paid to that sort of thing. But since then, with the lowering of currencies in continental Europe, with costs of production fluctuating as they did, it became essential to apply this statute to which I have just referred, based as it is upon the domestic cost and the selling price of the commodity in the country of origin. Bearing that in mind, I am sure the hon. gentleman will realize that there is nothing new in investigations being carried on. In this case the order was issued that pending investigation certain rates of duty should be applied, which involved, of course, the application of the clauses of the statute to which the hon. gentleman has just referred. The result of the investigations was unfavourable to the importer. The dumping duty was removed and the circular went to the customs houses accordingly. Thus vanishes case No. 2. Case No. 3 will also vanish when I tell the hon. gentleman that the automobile interests concerned have decided to establish agencies for the sale of their product in Canada. They have done so, and up to the present time there is no evidence that the conditions to which the hon. gentleman has called attention prevail.
Now I wish to tell the hon. gentleman the principle upon which this administrative action was taken. In a falling market, with surplus production, dealers will offer their commodities for export consumption at a discount which they will not accord to their home consumers. A few months ago my attention was drawn to a particular case in which a Canadian merchant in the city of New York inquired the price at which he could secure silk hose. He was told the price; it was the domestic price. He was then asked where they were to be sold and he replied, in Canada; whereupon a much lower price was quoted. Now to meet that situation is not always easy. On the
IMr. Bennett.]
one hand the ultimate consumer says, "I should be permitted to acquire these goods at the lowest possible price, and if I am fortunate enough, because of surplus production, to acquire that surplus at a lower price than prevails in the country of production, that is all to my advantage." On the other hand, there is the class of Canadian who believes that you cannot maintain industry without variety; for variety is essential to national development. The population cannot all be fishermen or lumbermen or wheat growers; and if variety is necessary there must foe some stability in our industrial life. That stability is predicated upon a fair return to the producer, whoever ho may be. We should try to see that the farmer, who is the ultimate creator of most of our wealth, receives a fair return. We should try to have the lumberman and the miner, or anyone else engaged in any form of industry, given a fair return. If he does not get a fair return bankruptcy is inevitable; for no man should be in business without some profit, whether it be farming or lumbering or mining or anything else. Under these circumstances I think the committee will agree that some action had to be taken by this country. You could not deal by legislation with every specific case as it arose, and I may assure the committee that the action taken last fall was not taken without much consideration. I leave it to the committee, as I have left it on other occasions, to say how otherwise the situation could be met. A tariff would meet it within bounds, but to meet the extreme cases which I have put to the committee would involve a tariff so high as to make it ridiculous; it would amount in some instances to several hundred per cent. On the other hand I think it is fair to say that notwithstanding occasional outbursts to the contrary there is no hon. member of the committee who does not believe in a tariff of some kind. Certainly I do not think there is any hon. member in my sight who does.
The extent of the tariff depends on what you are endeavouring to do with it. If you seek to use a tariff merely for exploitation, to use the word "protection" in the large sense in which it is sometimes used, then you are wrong. If it is used to give the Canadian an even chance with those who are trying to take his market away from him, then I submit, as I have so often done, that no man properly can urge anything against it. We have endeavoured to meet the class of case where a reasonable rate of tariff fails to accomplish the purpose aimed at, where free-

Customs Tariff
dom of trade is impossible. We have been compelled to put a value for duty purposes upon that commodity in order that there may be some sort of protection to the Canadian engaged in that industry.
I shall not take up the time of the committee in explaining again the circumstances under which we fixed the rate of discount upon motor cars. It was bound to work some hardship on those who were willing to give any rate of discount in order to get rid of their product. If a man is quoting a rate of discount far beyond what may be regarded as reasonable, something should be done to protect the Canadian against such a practice. We fixed 20 per cent as the arbitrary rate of discount which should be allowed with respect to importations. I agree with the hon. member for Weyburn that in some instances higher discounts have been quoted, but a decision has to be made and a line has to be drawn. I think it is regarded by those who have studied the question that the rate we decided on is a fair one. I regret that at the present time most businesses are not making money; at any rate we fixed it at 20 per cent. I appreciate the point raised by the hon. member, but I think he will be able to ascertain that those who are interested have' established Canadian selling agencies to meet the situation. The effect of the new tariff on the higher priced cars may be such as to prove a strong case for an increase of the discount, but that matter will have to be considered on its merits. This is all I have to say regarding the three cases presented to the house by the hon. member. I think he will agree that two have disappeared entirely, and in respect to the third, the producer in the foreign country has met the situation by providing selling agencies in Canada.
Mr. Y'OUNG: I am not as much alarmed as my right hon. friend over imports at a time when most of our people cannot buy the clothing they need, the boots and shoes they need, the fuel they need or the hundred and one other things they require. I think it little short of a crime that they should be denied the opportunity to buy those things where they can.

Why can they not buy
them?

Largely because of the
tariff. -

Because they have no
work and have no money.
And one of the principal reasons why they have no work is the tariff.
If it were not for the tariff there would not be any work.

I am not alarmed at these things coming into the country. The more goods that come into the country, the more goods will be available for the use of our people. However, if our people were to be given the opportunity to get these goods for nothing, my right hon. friend would not allow them to come in. If our neighbours to the south offered to feed us, clothe us and house us for nothing, the right hon. gentleman would not have it.
That would be dumping.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Our self .respect probably would rebel.
We get the sunlight free and we do not rebel against that.
There is no dumping there.

No country is going to send goods in here for nothing. When we take the goods that are sent in we must produce others to send out to pay for them, so that the more goods we take the more employment there will be at home to produce the goods with which to make payment.
Oh, oh.

My hon. friends may laugh, but let one of them get up and disprove that statement. I am delighted to learn that the one instance has been eliminated, that an investigation was made and it was discovered that the charge that these people were dumping cartridges was unfounded and the dump duty is not being collected.
Speaking about baskets, my right hon. friend tells the committee that they were being sold at less than cost. I do not know whether or not his investigators were accurate.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The cost to the domestic consumer in the country of origin.

This company was selling these baskets in the United States, the country of production, at the same price as they were selling them to us. The American government was quite willing that that company should go on and operate, whether at a profit or loss. However, our government, taking a benevolent interest in the American manufacturer, say to him: You are not making enough profit, so you must charge Canadians more in order to make more profit. Can you conceive of anything more ridiculous.

No

The tariff law of this country is 'being set up and enforced for the sole purpose of guaranteeing profits to American manufacturers. Can you conceive of anything quite so ridiculous?
No.
Hon. members cannot, neither can I.
Did not the hon. member give his support to the Dunning budget?

There were no dumping
duties in the Dunning budget. What I am referring to is the amendments to the tariff which wrere not touched by the Dunning budget.
The hon. member is talking as a free trader; he never talked as a free trader when a member of the government.
The hon. member was not here at the time, so he does not know what I talked about.
But he is going to be here for a long time.

With regard to automobiles, my right hon. friend says that the difficulty has been overcome by the American manufacturers establishing agencies in Canada. That may be true as applied to automobiles, but every exporter of goods to this country cannot establish agencies here. A manufacturer of a small article cannot come over here and establish selling agencies in order to function in such a way as to escape the duty. The only remedy is to amend the act so that this cannot occur.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my desire to delay the committee, but one point has been brought out in the debate, especially in the remarks of the hon. member for Wey-burn (Mr. Young), to which I would like to refer. I think the committee is aware that I have no objection to a reasonable dumping law; in fact I applied it myself when I was at the head of the department. I do not intend to deal with the application of the dump where goods are brought into Canada to be sold at less than the cost of production, but I should like to refer to what might be termed a typical case, that of automibiles. I am speaking of the importation of automobiles at normal prices and in normal times, not in times of over-production or slaughter conditions in the country of origin. As explained by the hon. member for Weyburn and referred to by myself the other day, suppose an automobile is invoiced at a list price of $1,000. With a bona fide discount of

30 per cent the car will be billed at $700 net to the dealer in Canada. But the Dominion government or the Department of National Revenue has decided that the fixed discount for purposes of duty shall be only 20 per cent. That means that the discount allowable for duty purposes is only $200 although the actual discount to the Canadian dealer is $300. In other words, although the price at which the automobile enters Canada is really $700, the Department of National Revenue applies the tariff on the sum of $800. That makes the duty higher. I have no fault to find with the fixing of the discount at 20 per cent, but it seems to me that it is going far enough to collect an additional duty on the extra $100, the result of the reduction of the discount from 30 per cent to 20 per cent. The point I want to make particularly is that made by the hon. member for Weyburn. It surely would be a pity if the Canadian dealer, in order to escape paying the dumping duty of $100, the difference between the actual price of $700 and the amount of $800 fixed by the department as the value for duty were to pay that extra $100 to the United States dealer, who does not really want it because he is getting sufficient profit when he sells the car at $700. Surely some other means could be found to serve the purpose the government has in view. The Minister of Finance says that what is suggested does not happen; that the United States automobile manufacturers will overcome that by establishing their own branches in Canada. That may be true in a practical sense.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I mean sales branches.

The dumping duty of which I have spoken may never have been applied; I do not know. But I doubt whether every automobile manufacturer in the United States would or could establish or find it worth while to establish his own branch in Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What I meant was not manufacturing branches but sales branches.

I understand. The manufacturer in the United States must of necessity be the proprietor of that branch and, I suppose, take a loss in his Canadian branch because he can only get a 30 per cent discount by establishing his own branch.
The same principle will apply not only to automobiles bu,t to any other commodity. In September last 'the government did two things affecting the importation of automobiles. By order in council they gave authority to the Minister of National Revenue to fix any value for duty on any commodity

Customs Tariff
imported, and on automobiles they fixed the discount at 20 per cent. I think the minister will agree that if in regard not only to automobiles but to other commodities as well that heavy dumping duty is charged as a result of fixing an arbitrary value, it will indeed be unfortunate, particularly if the money goes into the pocket of the foreign manufacturer rather than into the treasury of Canada. It occurs to me, that since the government have taken the power to fix values they might say this: We will fix values of automobiles, if you like, at such a sum that when the regular tariff rate is applied it will serve our purpose without our having to apply the dumping duty. I was going to make this suggestion for the consideration of the minister, that where an arbitrary value has already been fixed at a point sufficiently high for all practical purposes, the dumping duty should not apply. That would avoid all possibility of those moneys going into the pockets of the United States manufacturer rather than into the Dominion treasury, and would at the same time serve the purpose of protecting the Canadian manufacturer of automobiles or of any other commodity.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend remembers the difficulty he had in dealing with fruits and vegetables, a difficulty which he overcame practically by utilizing the dumping duty-although he called it by another name. Fruits and vegetables cannot be successfully dealt with unless recourse is had to the principle involved in the dumping duty. What the hon. member has said relates to a matter that has seriously engaged the attention of the government, as to just how it can be met and made of universal application, which is what one should endeavour to attain. Except in the manner I have indicated, we have not yet been able to discover a more suitable method.
I quite appreciate the difficulties that arise in the administration of the act-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: These are emergent conditions.

-but there should be no great difficulty-if there is an emergency or if it is desired to give protection without raising the tariff rate-in fixing the value at such a figure that the purpose will 'be served without the necessity of applying that excessive- for it is excessive-dumping duty.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Automobiles happen to be a commodity in regard to which there are serious difficulties, because they are charged on a list price, and you cannot very well fix for duty, as you can in connection with other commodities, a price at variance with the list price. My hon. friend is quite familiar with the difficulty, and I do not in any sense minimize it. But I know of no method of universal application of dealing with it except that which I indicated last fall, again a few days ago, and again to-night.

The Minister of Finance
spoke of United States manufacturers of automobiles establishing their own sales agencies in Canada. I suppose when they did that they dismissed all their Canadian agents.

I refer to a Canadian dealer in automobiles having the agency for two or three makes in the United States. Was he notified that his services would no longer be required because they were now going to open branches of their own?
